81. Choose Your Weapons Carefully, Relinquish Them Reluctantly

作者：Chad LaVigne

As seasoned veterans of software design and implementation, all architects are armed with an array of weapons they’ve used with repeated success. For one reason or another, these technologies have found favor and bubbled to the top of our list of preferred solutions. Most likely they’ve earned their rightful place in your arsenal by defeating fierce competition. Despite this, a barrage of new technologies constantly threatens their position. We are often compelled to lay down our weapons of choice for these new alternatives, but don’t be too quick to dismiss your trusty armaments. To cast them aside for alternatives that haven’t been proven through similar trials is a risky proposition.

作为软件设计和实现的老兵，所有架构师都带着一批反复成功使用的武器。由于某种原因，这些技术受青睐、冒泡到我们偏好方案列表顶部。它们很可能通过击败激烈竞争赢得了在你武器库中的正当位置。尽管如此，一连串新技术不断威胁它们的位置。我们经常被迫为这些新替代品放下选好的武器，但不要太快丢弃你可信赖的军备。为没经过类似考验的替代品把它们扔到一边是冒险之举。

This doesn’t mean that, once established on our list of favorites, a technology is granted infinite tenure and it certainly doesn’t mean that you can bury your head in the sand and ignore advancements in software development. For each technology, a time will come when it needs to be replaced. Technology moves quickly, and superior solutions are on the way. As architects we need to stay abreast of industry trends, but we don’t need to be the first to embrace fledgling technology. There’s usually no huge advantage to being the first to adopt new technology, but there can be several drawbacks.

这不意味着一旦上了最爱列表，技术就获得终身教职；当然也不意味着你可以埋头沙子、无视软件开发进步。对每个技术，它需要被替换的时候会来。技术发展快，更优方案在路上。作为架构师我们需要跟上行业趋势，但不需要做第一个拥抱萌芽技术的人。第一个采用新技术通常没有巨大优势，但可能有几个缺点。

To justify the risk involved with selecting new technology, its benefits should be a quantum leap forward. Many new technologies claim such advancement, but few deliver it. It’s easy to look at new technology and see technical advantages, but those benefits are often difficult to sell to stakeholders. Before you decide to blaze a trail with new technology, ask yourself how the business will benefit from this decision. If the best outcome from a business perspective is that no one will notice, rethink your decision.

为证明选新技术的风险合理，它的好处应该是量子级飞跃。很多新技术声称这种进步，但很少兑现。看新技术看到技术优势容易，但那些好处经常难卖给干系人。在决定用新技术开路前，问问自己业务会从这个决定怎么受益。如果业务角度最好结果是没人会注意，重新考虑你的决定。

Another important thing to acknowledge is the cost associated with the shortcomings of new technology. These costs can be high and are difficult to calculate. When you’re working with familiar technology you’re aware of its idiosyncrasies. It’s naïve to think that a new technology won’t come with its own collection of pitfalls. Adding problems that you haven’t solved before will destroy your estimates. You’re far more aware of the costs involved when implementing solutions using familiar technology.

另一个要承认的重要事情是新技术缺点关联的成本。这些成本可能高、难算。用熟悉技术时你知道它的特性。认为新技术不会自带一堆坑是天真的。加你以前没解决过的问题会毁掉你的估算。用熟悉技术实现方案时你对涉及的成本清楚得多。

One last thing to consider is future relevance. It would be nice if we could simply identify and select superior technologies, but things aren’t quite that simple. Great technologies don’t always win. Trying to predict the winners early is a gamble that doesn’t yield a large payoff. Wait for the hype to die down and see if the technology settles into a space of usefulness. You’ll find that many just go away. Don’t jeopardize your project for a technology that doesn’t have a future.

最后要考虑的是未来相关性。如果我们能简单识别和选优技术就好了，但事情没那么简单。伟大技术不总是赢。试图早期预测赢家是不会产生大回报的赌博。等炒作平息，看技术是否在有用空间安顿下来。你会发现很多就消失了。别为没有未来的技术危及你的项目。

Selecting the technologies we use to attack problems is a large part of the software architect’s job. Choose your weapons carefully and relinquish them reluctantly. Let your past success help to ensure future success, and evolve your technology stack cautiously.

选我们用来攻击问题的技术是软件架构师工作的很大一部分。仔细选武器，不情愿地放下。让你过去的成功帮确保未来成功，谨慎演化你的技术栈。

82. Your Customer Is Not Your Customer

作者：Eben Hewitt

As you work in requirements meetings to design software, pretend that your customer is not your customer. It turns out that this is a very easy thing to do, because it is true.

在需求会议里设计软件时，假装你的客户不是你的客户。事实证明这很容易做到，因为这是真的。

Your customer is not your customer. Your customer’s customer is your customer. If your customer’s customer wins, your customer wins. Which means you win.

你的客户不是你的客户。你客户的客户才是你的客户。如果你客户的客户赢了，你客户就赢。意味着你赢。

If you’re writing an e-commerce application, take care of the things that you know people who will shop at that site will need. They’ll need transport security. They’ll need encryption of stored data. Your customer may not mention these requirements. If you know that your customer is leaving out things your customer’s customer will need, address them, and communicate why.

如果你写电子商务应用，照顾你知道在那个网站购物的人会需要的东西。他们需要传输安全。他们需要存储数据加密。你的客户可能不提这些需求。如果你知道你的客户在漏掉你客户的客户会需要的东西，处理它们，并沟通为什么。

If your customer willingly and knowingly doesn’t care about certain important things that your customer’s customer cares about—as happens from time to time—consider stepping away from the project. Just because Sally Customer doesn’t want to pay for SSL every year and wants to store credit cards in plain text because it costs less to build, it’s not OK to simply agree. You’re killing your customer’s customer when you agree to do work you know is a bad idea.

如果你的客户明知且故意不关心你客户的客户关心的某些重要事——这种事时有发生——考虑离开项目。就因为 Sally 客户不想每年为 SSL 付钱、想明文存信用卡因为建起来便宜，简单同意是不对的。当你同意做你知道是坏主意的工作时，你在杀你客户的客户。

Requirements-gathering meetings are not implementation meetings. Forbid the customer’s use of implementation-specific terms unless it’s an absolute or well-understood problem. Allow your customer to express only the Platonic ideal, his concept and goals, rather than dictating a solution or even using technical terms.

需求收集会议不是实现会议。禁止客户用实现特定术语，除非是绝对或被充分理解的问题。允许你的客户只表达柏拉图式理想、他的概念和目标，而不是 dictate 一个方案甚至用技术术语。

So, how do you maintain such discipline in these meetings, which can be deceptively difficult? Remember to care for your customer’s customer. Remember that while your customer is writing your check, you must be clear that you need to honor best practices, so that you can make what the customer really needs, not just what they say they need. Of course, this takes lots of discussion, and clarity as to exactly what you’re doing and why.

那你怎么在这些会议里保持这种纪律——它们可能 deceptively 难？记住照顾你客户的客户。记住虽然你的客户在给你开支票，你必须清楚你需要尊重最佳实践，这样才能做客户真正需要的，而不只是他们说需要的。当然，这需要大量讨论，以及你到底在做什么、为什么的清晰。

Perhaps, as with so many things in life, this is best clarified by a poem. In 1649, Richard Lovelace wrote “To Lucasta, on Going to the Wars.” It ends with the line: “I could not love thee, dear, so much,/Loved I not honor more.”

也许，像生活中很多事一样，这最好用一首诗澄清。1649 年，Richard Lovelace 写了《致 Lucasta，奔赴战场》。结尾是：「我不能爱你这么多，亲爱的，若不是我更爱荣誉。」

We cannot love our customers so much, love we not their customers more.

我们不能这么爱客户，若不是我们更爱他们的客户。

83. It Will Never Look Like That

作者：Peter Gillard-Moss

It will never look like that. It is all too easy to fall into the trap of investing large amounts of time in a design and being confident that the implementation will come out the same. A detailed design can easily fool you into believing you have every angle covered. The greater the detail and the more in-depth the research, the greater your confidence in it. But it is an illusion: it will never look like that.

它永远不会那样。掉进在设计里投大量时间、自信实现会出来一样的陷阱太容易了。详细设计很容易骗你相信每个角度都覆盖了。细节越多、研究越深，你对它的信心越大。但这是幻觉：它永远不会那样。

The truth is, no matter how in-depth, how well researched, and how well thought-out your design, it will never come out looking the same as in your head. Something will happen, an external factor may affect the design: incorrect information, a limitation, an odd behaviour in someone else’s code. Or you may have got something wrong: an oversight, an incorrect presumption, a subtle concept missed. Or something will change: the requirements, the technology, or someone may just find a better way™.

事实是，不管你的设计多深入、多好研究、多深思熟虑，它出来永远不会和你脑子里一样。会有事发生，外部因素可能影响设计：错误信息、限制、别人代码里的奇怪行为。或者你可能搞错了：疏忽、错误假设、漏掉微妙概念。或者事情会变：需求、技术、或有人可能 just 找到更好方式™。

Those minor alterations in the design soon stack up and lots of minor alterations soon require that one big one has to be made. Before long your original concept is on the floor in pieces, and it’s back to the drawing board. You decide what you needed was more design and more detail, so back you go, and the next architectural vision is clearer, more radical, more perfect than the last.

设计里那些小改动很快堆积，很多小改动很快要求做一个大的。不久你最初的概念碎在地上，回到制图板。你决定你需要的是更多设计和更多细节，于是你回去，下一个架构愿景比上一个更清晰、更激进、更完美。

But before long the same thing happens. Those changes start to appear and shift your design, and developers keep shoving in more and more stuff trying their best to work around the broken design but just breaking it more, and you end up screaming, “Of course it’s got bugs; it was never designed to do that!”

但不久同样的事发生。那些改动开始出现、移动你的设计，开发不断塞进来更多东西，尽力绕着破碎设计工作但只是更破它，最后你尖叫：「它当然有 bug；它从来不是设计来做那个的！」

Design is a discovery process; as we implement, we discover new information that is often impossible to know upfront. By accepting that design is an ongoing and empirical process in a forever-changing world, we learn that the design process must be flexible and ongoing, too. Clinging to your original designs and trying to force them through is only going to produce one result, so you need to understand that it will never look like that .

设计是发现过程；我们实现时发现新信息，经常前期不可能知道。通过接受设计是永恒变化世界里持续、经验性的过程，我们学到设计过程也必须灵活、持续。紧抓你最初设计、试图强推只会产生一个结果，所以你需要理解它永远不会那样。

Peter Gillard-Moss Peter Gillard-Moss is a ThoughtWorker and general memeologist living in the U.K. He has worked in IT since 2000 on many projects, from public-facing websites in media and e-commerce to rich-client banking applications and corporate intranets.

Peter Gillard-Moss Peter Gillard-Moss 是 ThoughtWorker、住在英国的 meme 学家。他从 2000 年起在 IT 做过很多项目，从媒体和电子商务的面向公众网站到富客户端银行应用和企业内联网。

84. Choose Frameworks That Play Well with Others

作者：Eric Hawthorne

When choosing software frameworks as a basis of your system, you must consider not only the individual quality and features of each framework, but also how well the set of frameworks that make up your system will work together, and how easy it will be to adapt them to new software you may need to add as your system evolves. This means you must choose frameworks that do not overlap and that are humble, simple, and specialized.

选软件框架作为系统基础时，你不仅要考虑每个框架的单独质量和特性，还要考虑组成你系统的这组框架协作得多好，以及它们多容易适应你系统演化时可能需要加的新软件。这意味着你必须选不重叠、谦卑、简单、专门化的框架。

It is best if each framework or third-party library addresses a separate logical domain or concern, and does not tread into the domain or concern of another framework you need to use.

最好每个框架或第三方库处理单独的逻辑域或关注点，不踏入你需要用的另一个框架的域或关注点。

Make sure you understand how the logical domains and concerns addressed by your candidate frameworks overlap. Draw a Venn diagram if you need to. Two data models that overlap substantially in domain, or two implementations that address very similar concerns but in slightly different ways, will cause unnecessary complexity: the slight differences in conceptualization or representation must be mapped or patched with kludgy glue code. Chances are, you’ll end up not only with complex glue, but also with the lowest-common-denominator of the functionality or representative power of the two frameworks.

确保你理解候选框架处理的逻辑域和关注点怎么重叠。需要的话画维恩图。两个域大幅重叠的数据模型，或以略不同方式处理非常相似关注点的两个实现，会造成不必要复杂度：概念化或表示的细微差别必须用笨拙胶水代码映射或补丁。很可能最后你不仅有复杂胶水，还有两个框架功能或表示能力的最小公分母。

To minimize the chance that any given framework will overlap with another framework, choose frameworks that have a high utility-to-baggage ratio, in the context of your system requirements. Utility is the functionality or data

为最小化任何给定框架和另一个框架重叠的机会，在你系统需求上下文里选有效载荷/包袱比高的框架。效用是你项目从框架需要的功能或数据

representation that your project needs from the framework. Baggage is the framework’s sweeping, all-encompassing, I’m-in-charge view of the world. Does it insist on mixing data representation and control? Does its data model or set of packages and classes extend well beyond what your system needs? Do you have to become a fundamentalist in the framework’s religion, and limit your choices of other frameworks to those of the correct denomination? Does its excess complexity limit the kinds of things you can mix with it? If a framework comes with lots of baggage, then that it had also better be providing 75% of the functionality value in your project.

表示。包袱是框架那横扫一切、全包、我来负责的世界观。它坚持混合数据表示和控制吗？它的数据模型或包类集远超你系统需要吗？你必须变成框架宗教的原教旨主义者、把其他框架选择限制到正确教派吗？它的过度复杂度限制了你能和它混合的东西种类吗？如果一个框架带很多包袱，那它最好也提供你项目里 75% 的功能价值。

Your system should be comprised of mutually exclusive frameworks, each of which may be a master of its domain, but which is also simple, humble, and flexible.

你的系统应该由互斥框架组成，每个可能是其域的大师，但也简单、谦卑、灵活。

Eric Hawthorne Eric Hawthorne has architected, designed, and developed object-oriented software and distributed systems professionally since 1988, beginning and for 10 years at Macdonald Dettwiler, a Canadian systems-engineering company, where among other things, he had the opportunity to absorb some architectural technique from Philippe Kruchten.

Eric Hawthorne Eric Hawthorne 从 1988 年起专业架构、设计、开发面向对象软件和分布式系统，在加拿大系统工程公司 Macdonald Dettwiler 工作了 10 年，其间有机会从 Philippe Kruchten 那里吸收一些架构技术。

85. Make a Strong Business Case

作者：Yi Zhou

As a software architect, have you had a hard time getting your architecture project well funded? The benefits of software architecture are obvious for architects, but are mythical for many stakeholders. Mass psychology tells us that “seeing is believing” is the strongest belief for most people. At the early phase of the projects, however, there is little to demonstrate to convince stakeholders of the value of sound software architecture. It’s even more challenging in the nonsoftware industries where most stakeholders have little softwareengineering knowledge.

作为软件架构师，你有没有难以为你的架构项目争取到好资金？软件架构的好处对架构师显而易见，但对很多干系人是神话。大众心理学告诉我们「眼见为实」是大多数人最强的信念。然而项目早期，几乎没什么可展示来说服干系人好软件架构的价值。在非软件行业更具挑战，那里大多数干系人几乎没有软件工程知识。

Mass psychology also shows that most people believe in “perception is reality.” Therefore, if you can control how people perceive the architectural approach you propose, it’s virtually guaranteed that you can control how they will react to your proposal. How can you mange stakeholders’ perceptions? Make a strong business case for your architecture. People who have the budget authority to sponsor your ideas are almost always business-driven.

大众心理学还显示大多数人相信「感知即现实」。因此，如果你能控制人们怎么感知你提议的架构方法，几乎可以保证你能控制他们怎么反应你的提议。你怎么管理干系人的感知？为你的架构做一个强商业案例。有预算权赞助你想法的人几乎总是业务驱动的。

I have employed the following five steps to generate solid business cases to successfully sell my architectural approach many times in my career:

我在职业生涯里多次用以下五步生成扎实商业案例成功卖出我的架构方法：

Establish the 1. value proposition . The value proposition is your executive summary of why your organization’s business warrants a particular software architecture. The key for this is to compare your architectural approach with existing solutions or other alternatives. The focus should be put on its capability to increase the productivity and efficiency of the business rather than how brilliant the technologies are.

建立价值主张。价值主张是你组织业务为什么需要特定软件架构的执行摘要。关键是把你的架构方法和现有方案或其他替代品比较。焦点应放在它提升业务生产力和效率的能力上，而不是技术多辉煌。

Build 2. metrics to quantify. The values you promise to deliver need to be quantified to a reasonable extent. The more you measure, the more you can bolster your case that sound architecture will lead to a substantial return. The earlier you establish metrics, the better you manage people’s perceptions that help you sell responsible architecture.

建可量化的指标。你承诺交付的价值需要合理程度量化。你测量越多，越能支持你的论点：好架构会带来实质回报。你越早建立指标，越好管理人们的感知，帮你卖出负责任的架构。

Link back to traditional business measures. 3. It would be ideal if you can translate your technical analysis into dollar figures. After all, the only constant parameter in the traditional business measures is money. Find business analysts as your partners if you are not comfortable with financial work.

链回传统业务指标。如果你能把技术分析翻译成美元数字，那理想。毕竟传统业务指标里唯一恒定参数是钱。如果你不熟悉财务工作，找业务分析师做伙伴。

Know where to stop. 4. Before you know where to stop, you need to prepare a roadmap that captures a vision with each milestone on it tied directly to business values. Let the stakeholders decide where to stop. If the business value for each momentum is significant, you’re most likely to get continued funding.

知道在哪停。知道在哪停之前，你需要准备一个路线图，捕捉愿景，每个里程碑直接绑业务价值。让干系人决定在哪停。如果每个动量的业务价值显著，你最可能拿到持续资金。

Find the right timing. 5. Even if you follow the previous four steps to generate a solid business case, you still may not be able to sell your ideas if you pick the bad timing. I remember one of my proposals did not get approved for a long time until another project turned out to be a total failure because of poor architectural design. Be smart on timing.

找对时机。即使你按前四步生成扎实商业案例，如果时机不对你仍可能卖不出想法。我记得我的一个提议很久没批，直到另一个项目因为差架构设计彻底失败。时机要聪明。

86. Control the Data, Not Just the Code

作者：Chad LaVigne

Source code control and continuous integration are excellent tools for managing the application build and deployment process. Along with source code, schema and data changes are often a significant part of this process and thus warrant similar controls. If your build and deployment process includes a list of elaborate steps required for data updates, beware. These are the lists that always have you crossing your fingers. They look something like this:

源码控制和持续集成是管理应用构建部署过程的优秀工具。连同源码，schema 和数据变更经常是这个过程的重要部分，因此需要类似控制。如果你的构建部署过程包括一长串数据更新要做的精心步骤，当心。这些就是那种让你 crossing fingers 的列表。它们看起来像这样：

Create a list of scripts that need to be run, in order. 1.

1. 按顺序创建需要运行的脚本列表。

E-mail scripts to special database person. 2.

2. 把脚本邮件发给特殊数据库人员。

Database person copies the scripts to a location where they’re executed by 3. a cron job.

3. 数据库人员把脚本拷到 cron job 执行的位置。

Check script execution log and pray that all scripts ran successfully since 4. you’re not exactly sure what will happen if you rerun them.

4. 检查脚本执行日志，祈祷所有脚本成功跑——因为你不太确定重跑会怎样。

Run validation scripts and spot-check the data. 5.

5. 跑验证脚本并抽查数据。

Regression test the application and see what blows up. 6.

6. 对应用做回归测试，看什么炸。

Write scripts to insert missing data and fix blow-ups. 7.

7. 写脚本插入缺失数据、修爆炸。

Repeat. 8.

8. 重复。

OK, so that might be a slight exaggeration but it’s not that far off. Many a project requires this type of acrobatic workflow for successful database migration.

好吧这可能有点夸张但离得不远。很多项目需要这种杂技工作流才能成功数据库迁移。

For some reason the data portion of the migration plan seems to be easily overlooked during architecture planning. As a result, it can become a brittle, manual process that gets bolted on as an afterthought.

出于某种原因，迁移计划的数据部分在架构规划时容易被忽略。结果，它可能变成脆弱、手动过程，作为事后想法 bolt 上去。

This complex web-work creates many opportunities for process breakdown. To make matters worse, bugs caused by schema and data changes don’t always get caught by unit tests as part of the nightly build report. They like to rear their ugly head in a loud, boisterous manner immediately after a build has been migrated. Database problems are usually tedious to reverse by hand and their solutions tend to be more difficult to validate. The value of a completely automated build process that is capable of restoring the database to a known state will never be more evident than when you’re using it to fix an extremely visible issue. If you don’t have the ability to drop the database and restore it to a state that is compatible with a specific build of the application, you are susceptible to the same type of problems you’d have if you couldn’t back out a code change quickly.

这个复杂蜘蛛网制造很多流程崩溃机会。更糟的是，schema 和数据变更导致的 bug 不总被 nightly build 报告里的单元测试抓住。它们喜欢在构建刚迁移后立刻以响亮、喧闹的方式抬头。数据库问题手动回滚通常乏味，它们的方案更难验证。一个能把数据库恢复到已知状态的完全自动化构建过程的价值，在你用它修一个极其显眼问题时最明显。如果你不能 drop 数据库并恢复到和应用特定构建兼容的状态，你就容易受到和不能快速回退代码变更时同类问题的影响。

Database changes shouldn’t create a ripple in your build’s time-space continuum. You need to be able to build the entire application, including the database, as one unit. Make data and schema management a seamless part of your automated build and testing process early on and include an undo button; it will pay large dividends. At best it will save hours of painful, high-stress problem solving after a late night blunder. At worst it will give your team the ability to confidently charge forward with refactoring of the data access layer.

数据库变更不应该在你构建的时空连续体里制造涟漪。你需要能把整个应用包括数据库作为一个单元构建。尽早让数据和 schema 管理成为自动化构建测试过程无缝部分，并加一个 undo 按钮；它会付大红利。最好它能在深夜 blunder 后省几小时痛苦高压问题解决。最坏它给你团队自信推进重构数据访问层的能力。

87. Pay Down Your Technical Debt

作者：Burkhardt Hufnagel

On any project that is in production (i.e., it has customers that are using it), there will come a time when a change must be made; either a bug needs fixing, or a new feature must be added. At that point there are two possible choices: you can take the time needed to “do it right,” or you can take one or more “shortcuts” and try to get the change out the door sooner.

任何在生产中的项目（也就是有客户在用），总有一天要做变更；要么修 bug，要么加新功能。那时有两个可能选择：你可以花时间「做对」，或者你可以走一个或多个「捷径」、试图早点把变更弄出门。

Generally, the business people (sales/marketing and customers) will want the change made as quickly as possible, while the developers and testers will be more interested in taking the time to properly design, implement, and test the change before delivering it to the customers.

通常业务人员（销售/市场和客户）想尽快做变更，而开发和测试更想在交付客户前花时间正确设计、实现和测试变更。

As the project’s architect, you’ll have to decide which makes more sense and then convince the decision makers to take your advice; and, as with most architectural issues, there is a tradeoff involved. If you believe the system is reasonably stable, then it may make sense to go the “quick and dirty” route and get the change into production quickly. That’s fine, but you need to know that in doing so your project is incurring some “technical debt” that must be repaid later. Repayment, in this case, means going back and making the change in the way you would have if you’d had the time and resources to do it right the first time.

作为项目架构师，你得决定哪个更合理，然后说服决策者听你的建议；和大多数架构问题一样，这里涉及权衡。如果你相信系统 reasonably 稳定，那走「快而脏」路线、快速把变更进生产可能合理。那没问题，但你需要知道这么做你的项目在累积一些以后必须还的「技术债」。还，在这个案例里，意味着回去以你第一次有时间资源做对时会用的方式做变更。

So why the concern over making changes properly now versus later? It’s because there’s a hidden cost to making these quick and dirty fixes. For financial debts the hidden cost is called “interest,” and most anyone with a credit card knows

那为什么关心现在对 vs 以后做变更？因为做这些快而脏的修复有隐藏成本。金融债里隐藏成本叫「利息」，任何有信用卡的人都知道

how expensive just paying the interest on a debt can be. For technical debt, interest takes the form of instability in the system, and increased maintenance costs due to the hacked-in changes and lack of proper design, documentation, and/or tests. And, like financial interest, regular payments must be made until the original debt is repaid.

只付债务利息能多贵。技术债里，利息以系统不稳定的形式出现，以及因为 hacked-in 变更和缺乏正确设计、文档和/或测试而增加的维护成本。而且，像金融利息一样，必须定期付，直到原始债还完。

Now that you understand a bit more about the true cost of technical debt, you might decide the price is too high and you can’t afford the cost. But when it’s a choice between having the developers get the fix out as quickly as possible or taking a severe financial hit, it generally makes sense to get the fix out quickly. So, take the hit and get the change into production ASAP, but don’t stop there.

现在你多懂了点技术债的真实成本，你可能觉得价格太高、承担不起。但当选择是让开发尽快出修复还是承受严重财务打击，通常快速出修复合理。所以，承受打击尽快把变更进生产，但别停在那。

Once the fix is in production, have the developers go back and fix it properly so that it can be included in the next scheduled release. This is the equivalent of charging something on your credit card and then paying off the balance at the end of the month so you don’t get charged interest. This way you can provide the fast changes the business needs, while keeping your project out of debtor’s prison.

修复进生产后，让开发回去正确修它，这样它能进下一个计划发布。这相当于刷信用卡然后月底还清余额、不被收利息。这样你可以提供业务需要的快速变更，同时不让项目进债务人监狱。

Burkhardt Hufnagel Burk Hufnagel has been creating positive user experiences since 1978 and is a lead software architect at LexisNexis.

Burkhardt Hufnagel Burk Hufnagel 从 1978 年起创造积极用户体验，是 LexisNexis 的首席软件架构师。

88. Don't Be a Problem Solver

作者：Eben Hewitt

With some exceptions, architects used to be developers. Developers get rewarded for solving programming problems, which are more local in scope than architectural problems. Many programming problems are small, tricky, algorithmic problems. Such problems are frequently presented in programming interviews, books, and university courses as if the problems exist in a vacuum. The trickiness is alluring and seductive. Over time, we begin to accept such problems out of hand. We do not ask if this problem is meaningful, or interesting, or useful, or ethical. We are not rewarded for considering the relation of this problem to a larger landscape. We are trained to focus only on our solution, which is aggravated by the fact that solving hard problems is hard. We leap into action in programming interviews, which often begin by presenting us with some number of jelly beans we are meant to sort according to an arbitrary set of constraints. We learn not to question the constraints; they are a pedagogical tool, intended to lead us to discover what the teacher or interviewer or mentor already knows.

除了一些例外，架构师曾经是开发。开发因解决编程问题受奖励，这些问题范围比架构问题更局部。很多编程问题是小、棘手、算法问题。这种问题经常在编程面试、书、大学课程里呈现，好像问题存在于真空中。棘手迷人、诱人。久而久之我们开始不加思索接受这种问题。我们不问这个问题是否有意义、有趣、有用、道德。我们因为考虑这个问题和更大图景的关系而受奖励。我们被训练只聚焦我们的方案，而解决难题很难这一事实加剧了这点。我们在编程面试里跃入行动，面试通常先给我们一些糖豆让我们按任意约束排序。我们学会不质疑约束；它们是教学工具，意在引导我们发现老师/面试官/导师已经知道的。

Architects and developers learn to enter problem-solving mode immediately. But sometimes the best solution is no solution. Many software problems need not be solved at all. They only appear as problems because we look only at the symptoms.

架构师和开发学会立刻进入问题解决模式。但有时最好的方案是没方案。很多软件问题根本不需要解决。它们看起来像问题只是因为我们只看症状。

Consider managed memory. Developers on managed platforms have not solved memory problems, nor could many of them do so if required; part of their solution means that they mostly just don’t have that problem.

想想托管内存。托管平台上的开发没有解决内存问题，很多人如果被要求也解决不了；他们的方案一部分意味着他们大多根本没那个问题。

Consider complex builds that demand lots of interconnected scripts requiring the enforcement of many standards and conventions. You could solve that

想想复杂构建，它要求很多互联脚本、强制很多标准和惯例。你可以解决那个

problem, and it would feel great to get it all to work, putting your best scripting skills and best practices to work. Our colleagues will be impressed. No one is impressed by us not solving a problem. But if we can step back and figure out that we aren’t solving a build problem but rather an automation and portability problem, this might lead you to a tool that abstracts it away.

问题，把它全搞起来感觉会很棒，用上你最好的脚本技能和最佳实践。我们的同事会被 impress。没人因为我们不解决问题而 impress。但如果我们退一步搞清楚我们不是在解决构建问题而是自动化和可移植性问题，这可能引你到一个把它抽象掉的工具。

Because architects tend to immediately enter problem-solving mode, we forget, or rather have never learned how, to interrogate the problem itself. We must learn, like a telephoto lens, to zoom in and zoom out, in order to ensure that the question is really framed properly, and that we’re not merely accepting what we’re given. We must not be passive receptacles for requirements, cheerfully ready at our posts, handing out our smartest solutions in the manner of a Pez dispenser.

因为架构师倾向立刻进入问题解决模式，我们忘了——或者说从没学过怎么——审问问题本身。我们必须学会像长焦镜头一样 zoom in/out，确保问题真的被正确框定，我们不只是接受给我们的东西。我们不能是需求的被动容器，在岗位上兴高采烈、像 Pez 糖果分配器一样发出我们最聪明的方案。

Instead of immediately working to solve the problem as presented, see if you can change the problem. Ask yourself, what would the architecture look like if I just didn’t have this problem? This can lead ultimately to more elegant and sustainable solutions. The business problem still does need to be solved, but not, perhaps, as immediately suggested.

不要立刻按呈现的问题解决，看你能不能改变问题。问问自己：如果我根本没这个问题，架构会什么样？这最终可能导向更优雅可持续的方案。业务问题仍需要解决，但也许不像立刻建议的那样。

We have to break our addiction to “problems.” We love to get them, seeing ourselves on a European bridge, as if we are secret agents who’ve just been handed a self-destructing brown envelope containing our mission. Before considering your answer to a problem, think what the world would look like if you just didn’t have this problem.

我们必须打破对「问题」的瘾。我们喜欢接到问题，把自己想象在欧洲桥上，像特工刚接到装着任务的自毁棕色信封。在考虑你对问题的答案前，想想如果你根本没这个问题世界会什么样。

89. Build Systems to Be Zuhanden

作者：Keith Braithwaite

We build tools. The systems that we make have no other reason to exist (nor we to get paid) than to help someone, usually someone else, do something.

我们造工具。我们做的系统没有别的存在理由（我们也没有别的拿工资理由），就是帮某个人——通常是别人——做某事。

Martin Heidegger, an influential German philosopher of the 20th century, explored the ways that people experience tools (and more generally “equipment”) in their lives. People use tools to work toward a goal, and the tool is merely a means to an end.

Martin Heidegger，20 世纪有影响的德国哲学家，探索了人们在生活中体验工具（更广义「设备」）的方式。人们用工具朝目标工作，工具只是手段。

During successful use, a tool is zuhanden (“ready-to-hand,” having the property of “handiness”). The tool is experienced directly; it is used without consideration, without theorisation. We grasp the tool and use it to move toward our goal. In use, it vanishes! The tool becomes an extension of the user’s body and is not experienced in its own right. One sign of a tool being zuhanden is that it becomes invisible, unfelt, insignificant.

在成功使用中，工具是 zuhanden（「上手」，有「称手」属性）。工具被直接体验；不经考虑、不经理论化就被用。我们抓住工具用它朝目标移动。使用中它消失了！工具成为用户身体的延伸，不被自身体验。工具 zuhanden 的一个标志是它变得不可见、无感觉、不重要。

Consider what it feels like to hammer a nail or to write with a pen. Think about that immediacy. Think about the way the tool seems to be a seamless extension of your body.

想想锤钉子或用笔写字什么感觉。想想那种即时性。想想工具好像你身体无缝延伸的方式。

Alternatively, and usually when something has gone wrong with it, the user may experience a tool as vorhanden (“present-at-hand”). The tool is isolated from the goal; it lies before us demanding attention. It becomes a topic of investigation in its own right. The user is no longer able to proceed toward his goal but must deal first with the tool, without it doing anything to move him toward his goal. As technologists we tend to experience the systems we build for users as vorhanden while we build them, and again when we receive defect reports. For us, the tool is quite properly an object of enquiry, of theorising, of investigation. It is a thing to be studied.

另一种情况——通常是它出问题时——用户可能把工具体验为 vorhanden（「在手边」/现成）。工具和目标隔离；它摆在我们面前要求注意。它本身成为调查主题。用户不能再朝目标前进，必须先处理工具，而它没做任何把他朝目标推的事。作为技术人，我们倾向于在构建时把为用户建的系统体验为 vorhanden，收到缺陷报告时又一次。对我们来说，工具很恰当地是探究、理论化、调查的对象。它是要被研究的东西。

However, it is crucial to their success that the users experience the tools we build for them as zuhanden. Are your systems architected to be invisible in use? Does the user interface fall naturally to hand? Or do your systems keep demanding attention, distracting users from their goal?

然而，对它们的成功至关重要的是用户把我们为他们建的工具体验为 zuhanden。你的系统架构成使用中不可见吗？用户界面自然到手吗？还是你的系统不断要求注意、把用户从目标分心？

90. Find and Retain Passionate Problem Solvers

作者：Chad LaVigne

Putting together a team  of outstanding developers is one of the most important things you can do to ensure the success of a software project. While the concept of keeping that team together does not seem to get as much lip service, it is equally important. Therefore, you need to carefully select your development team and diligently protect it once assembled.

组建一支优秀开发团队是你为确保软件项目成功能做的最重要事情之一。虽然留住团队这个概念似乎没得到那么多口头服务，它同等重要。因此你需要仔细选开发团队，一旦组建就勤奋保护它。

Most people probably agree that finding top-notch developers requires thorough technical interviewing. But what does thorough mean exactly? It doesn’t mean requiring candidates to answer difficult questions about obscure technical details. Screening for specific technical knowledge is definitely part of the process but turning an interview into a certification test will not guarantee success. You are searching for developers with problem-solving skills and passion. The tools you use are sure to change; you need people who are good at attacking problems regardless of the technologies involved. Proving someone has the ability to recite every method in an API tells you very little about that person’s aptitude or passion for solving problems.

大多数人可能同意找顶级开发需要彻底技术面试。但彻底到底什么意思？它不意味着要求候选人回答关于晦涩技术细节的难题。筛特定技术知识当然是过程一部分，但把面试变成认证考试不会保证成功。你在找有问题解决技能和热情的开发。你用的工具肯定会变；你需要不管涉及什么技术都擅长攻问题的人。证明某人能背 API 里每个方法，对这个人解决问题的资质或热情告诉很少。

However, asking someone to explain her approach to diagnosing a performance problem gives you great insight into her methods for problem solving. If you want to learn about a developer’s ability to apply lessons learned, ask what she would change given the chance to start her most recent project anew. Good developers are passionate about their work. Asking them about past experience will bring out that passion and tell you what correct answers to technical trivia questions cannot.

然而，让某人解释她诊断性能问题的方法，会让你深刻了解她的问题解决方法。如果你想了解开发应用教训的能力，问她如果有机会重新开始最近项目会改什么。好开发对工作有热情。问他们过去经验会带出热情，告诉你技术 trivia 正确答案不能告诉你的。

If you have been diligent in staffing a strong team, you want to do whatever is within your power to keep the team together. Retention factors such as compensation may be out of your hands, but make sure you’re taking care of the little things that help to foster a healthy work environment. Good developers are often strongly motivated by recognition. Use this fact to your advantage and acknowledge stellar performances. Finding great developers is difficult; letting people know they are valued is not. Don’t miss simple chances to build morale and boost productivity.

如果你勤奋配了强团队，你想做你能力范围内一切留住团队。像薪酬这样的保留因素可能不在你手里，但确保你在照顾帮助培养健康工作环境的小事。好开发经常被认可强烈激励。利用这个事实，表扬杰出表现。找好开发难；让人知道他们被重视不难。别错过建士气、提生产力的简单机会。

Be careful with negative reinforcement. Too much of it may stifle a developer’s creativity and reduce productivity. Worse yet, it’s likely to create dissension within the team. Good developers are smart; they know they’re not wrong all of the time. If you’re picking apart the minutiae of their work, you’ll lose their respect. Keep criticism constructive and don’t require that every solution look like it came from you.

小心负面强化。太多可能扼杀开发创造力、降生产力。更糟，它可能在团队里制造不和。好开发聪明；他们知道自己不总是错。如果你在挑他们工作的细节毛病，你会失去他们的尊重。保持批评建设性，不要要求每个方案都像你做的。

The importance of staffing your development team correctly can’t be overstated. These are the people who do the heavy lifting. When it comes to estimates, they’re all treated as equal producers. Make sure it’s tough to crack the starting lineup, and once you’ve got a winning team, go the extra mile to keep it together.

正确配开发团队的重要性怎么强调都不过分。这些人是做重活的。估算时他们都被当作平等生产者。确保首发阵容难进，一旦你有了赢的团队，多走一英里留住它。
